lesson.title: Splitting the Story: Oxidation and Reduction Half Reactions
lesson.summary: A half reaction isolates just the oxidation or just the reduction piece of a redox reaction, showing exactly how many electrons are lost or gained by each species.
lesson.body:
A redox reaction always contains two storylines running at once, one species losing electrons and another gaining them. Rather than trying to track both at the same time, chemists routinely split the overall equation into two half reactions, one written for oxidation and one for reduction, and analyze each on its own. This turns out to be far more manageable, especially once reactions involve polyatomic ions with several atoms whose oxidation numbers could plausibly be changing.

Take the zinc and copper reaction from the last chapter, Zn(s) + Cu2+(aq) is right arrow Zn2+(aq) + Cu(s), and split it. The oxidation half reaction isolates what happens to zinc: Zn is right arrow Zn2+ + 2e-. Check it on its own: 1 zinc atom on each side, and charge of 0 on the left equals charge of +2 plus 2 electrons at -1 each, which is +2 - 2 = 0, on the right. Balanced. The reduction half reaction isolates copper: Cu2+ + 2e- is right arrow Cu. Check it too: 1 copper atom each side, and charge of +2 - 2 = 0 on the left equals charge of 0 on the right, since copper metal is neutral. Also balanced.

Now add the two half reactions together, left sides together and right sides together: Zn + Cu2+ + 2e- is right arrow Zn2+ + 2e- + Cu. Notice that 2e- appears on both sides of this combined equation, since zinc released exactly the 2 electrons that copper absorbed. Electrons that appear identically on both sides cancel, the same way any species would in an ordinary equation, leaving Zn + Cu2+ is right arrow Zn2+ + Cu, which is exactly the overall redox equation you started with. This is the whole point of half reactions: write each one so it balances on its own, in atoms and in charge, and when you add them together with matching electron counts, the electrons vanish from the final equation and you are left with a correctly balanced overall reaction.

This split is not just a bookkeeping convenience either. In an electrochemical cell, like a battery, the oxidation half reaction and the reduction half reaction physically happen in different places, at two separate electrodes connected by a wire, which is how the cell forces electrons to flow through a circuit rather than hopping directly from one species to the other. That electrochemistry connection is a topic for another day, but it is worth knowing that half reactions are not just an algebra trick, they describe something physically real. For now, the important use of half reactions is as the foundation for a systematic method of balancing redox equations, which is exactly where the next chapter goes.
